\chapter{Cansado --- a State, Not a Quality}
\label{ch:cansado}
\hlchaptermodality{57}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say how I am right now with estar and an adjective.}

I can say how I am right now with estar and an adjective.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[cansado]{cansado}

\label{lesson:ES-C09-cansado}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}a big house.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Una casa grande}.) That is what the house \textbf{is}.

Now for something that is only true today.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{cansado}} — tired
\end{quote}

\emph{Cansado} comes from \emph{cansar}, to tire, and behind that is Latin \textbf{campsāre}: \emph{to turn aside off the road}. The tiredness is what made you turn off.

\textbf{And your decoder cannot help you here.} There is no English cousin to find — no \emph{cansate}, no \emph{campsation}. English took its word for this from an entirely different place.

That is worth meeting on purpose. The rules you built are a \textbf{lead}, not a guarantee, and a word that gives nothing back is not a failure of the method. It is simply one of the words you learn the ordinary way.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the state, not the quality}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{Estoy cansado.}} — not \emph{soy cansado}.
\end{quote}

You learned two verbs for \emph{to be}. Here is the first describing word that shows you why:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{Estoy cansado.} & I am tired — \textbf{today}. \\
\emph{Es grande.} & It is big — \textbf{that is what it is}. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Ser} is for what a thing is. \emph{Estar} is for how it is right now. Being tired is a state you are passing through, so it takes \emph{estar}, always.

And unlike \emph{grande}, this one \textbf{does} shift, because it ends in \emph{-o}:

\begin{quote}
\emph{Estoy cansad\textbf{o}}.  ·  \emph{Estoy cansad\textbf{a}}.
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Estoy cansado}
  \item \emph{La casa es grande, pero estoy cansado}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which verb for tired? (\emph{\textbf{Estar}}.) Why? (It is a \textbf{state}.)

And does \emph{cansado} shift for a woman? (\textbf{Yes} — \emph{cansada}, because it ends in \emph{-o}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
